'''Malcolm Bruce Smith''' (29 February 1924 – 27 July 2000) was an [[Australians|Australian]] chemist who studied the egg protein [[ovalbumin]]. He described the formation of S-ovalbumin from the native form (R-ovalbumin) as the pH of eggs rises over time.<ref>McKenzie, H.A. 2003. In Memoriam: Malcolm Bruce Smith, 29 February 1924 – 27 July 2000. Journal of Protein Chemistry 22:	205–206</ref>

Smith was raised and attended schools in [[Angaston, South Australia|Angaston]] and [[Nuriootpa, South Australia|Nuriootpa]] in [[South Australia]]. He won Country Scholarship to study [[Industrial Chemistry]] at the [[University of South Australia|South Australian School of Mines]] in [[Adelaide]].<ref>The Advertiser (Adelaide, SA : 1931–1954), Tuesday 7 February 1939, page 11</ref> His studies were interrupted by [[World War II]], when he was recruited to a laboratory position by the Munitions Department.<ref>Unpublished memoirs written by Malcolm Smith in about 1990</ref> 

After some years working for a public analyst in Adelaide, C.A.Smythe & Co, he was engaged by the Australian Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (later renamed the C.S.I.R.O) as a Technical Officer at the Division of Food Preservation and Transport in [[Sydney]].<ref>Letter of appointment dated 15 January 1947</ref> Smith remained in this employment until retiring on 29 February 1984 from the position of Principal Research Scientist at the then named Division of Food Research.<ref>This is recorded with an appreciation in the Division's News Journal published at that time</ref> 

Smith was co-author of a history of his Division, published in 1979.<ref>"Bastian JM, 1979, Fifty years of food research, CSIRO. Melbourne, Vic, CSIRO". {{ISBN|0 643 02524 3}}.</ref> He was awarded degrees of BSc and MSc at the [[University of New South Wales]] in 1956 and 1959, and was awarded the degree of Doctor of Science by that University in 1980. His discourse discussed his published research into 'Physico-Chemical Studies on Proteins, with Particular Reference to the Structure and Stability of Egg Proteins.'<ref>UNSW citation dated 9 October 1980. His submission for the degree cites 26 published articles</ref>

Smith married Josephine Lucy in Adelaide in 1945, and had two daughters and two sons. He died from [[Diffuse Lewy Body disease|diffuse lewy body disease]] in 2000.
